solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Cool bat has admirers (3,4)

annotation.surface: A cricket or baseball bat that is so stylish it has its own followers.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words read as adjective and noun, a cool bat, but each is a verb or thing in its own right: to fan cools, and a club is a bat.
annotation.definitionFit: The collective noun stands for the group: an organised body of devotees can be called simply its admirers.

entries.clue: Ready to fart with much energy? (4,2,5)

blocks.note: pulses are notorious for causing wind, so a stomach loaded with them is primed
an idiom for bouncy, lively high spirits

annotation.surface: A cheeky question about someone about to break wind.
annotation.walkthrough: The rude first reading is the literal one: a stomach full of beans. The idiom 'full of beans' means bursting with energy.
annotation.definitionFit: Literal and idiomatic senses: a belly stuffed with beans is primed for wind, and the everyday idiom means bouncy and lively.

entries.clue: Family member’s ‘bon voyage’ at last, with a sigh of relief (6)

indicatorNotes.at last: take the last letter of each word

blocks.note: last letters of boN and voyagE
phew is what you say when relieved

annotation.surface: A relative's departure is waved off with a farewell and a relieved sigh.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a guest you were glad to see go; 'at last' looks like 'finally gone' but picks the last letters of both words.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a brother's or sister's son is one particular relative.

entries.clue: Secures mantles for portraits? No! (10)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition works by contrast: landscape is the page orientation that is not portrait

blocks.note: to land a deal is to secure it
a mantle is a cloak or cape

annotation.surface: Someone buying cloaks to dress sitters for their portraits, then thinking better of it.
annotation.walkthrough: Pictures and page layouts come in two orientations, portrait and landscape; the 'No!' turns portraits into their opposite.
annotation.definitionFit: Defined by its opposite: pictures and page layouts are either tall portraits or wide scenes of countryside, so 'not portraits' points to the other kind.

entries.clue: See 1
Water bird and water city (7)

blocks.note: a swan is a water bird

annotation.surface: A list of waterside things: a bird and a coastal city.
annotation.walkthrough: SWANSEA is a coastal city in south Wales. 'Water city' reads as one phrase, but 'water' belongs to the wordplay and 'city' stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the Welsh port on the south coast is one example of a city.

entries.clue: More palatable rugby formation? Mister, that is welcomed (9)

indicatorNotes.welcomed: a host who welcomes a guest takes them inside, so MR takes IE in

blocks.note: a scrum is a set formation in rugby
Mr is the short form of Mister

annotation.surface: A rugby scrum is offered as tastier, and a man called Mister is made welcome.
annotation.walkthrough: SCRUMMY is informal British for delicious; the question mark flags the pun on scrum.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British synonym: the comparative of scrummy, nursery slang for delicious, means tastier.

entries.clue: Scotland’s rising voice (4)

indicatorNotes.’s: the answer belongs to the word, sitting inside it
indicatorNotes.rising: in a down clue the letters read upwards

annotation.surface: The voice of Scotland is rising, as in a national movement.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside SCOTLAND and read upwards in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the low female or high male singing range is one of the voice parts in a choir.

entries.clue: Careless error with footwear (8)

blocks.note: a slip is a small error

annotation.surface: A careless mistake made in the matter of shoes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Careless error' reads as one phrase, but 'Careless' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: originally wearing slippers, the word came to mean sloppy and slovenly.

entries.clue: Story one acted out (8)

indicatorNotes.out: out of order, so the letters are put out of their places

annotation.surface: A story that one person performed in front of others.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Acted out' looks like one phrasal verb, but 'out' alone is the instruction and 'acted' is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a short personal tale told in conversation is a story.

entries.clue: Type of flower or 4 (5)

blocks.note: a garden plant with tall spikes of blooms
a cross-reference to 4 down, whose answer is BEANS

annotation.surface: A choice between a flower and a cross-reference.
annotation.walkthrough: The number points at 4 down, BEANS: lupin seeds are eaten as beans.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: the tall-spiked garden flower, whose seeds are also eaten as pickled beans.

entries.clue: Refreshes vehicle for military attack (3,6)

blocks.note: to air a room is to freshen it

annotation.surface: A vehicle is spruced up for an offensive.
annotation.walkthrough: The pieces do not match the answer's two words: the S of the first word is borrowed by the second.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a bombing raid from aircraft is one kind of military attack.

entries.clue: Starts Google at last with identical password (4,6)

indicatorNotes.at last: 'at last' means at the very end, so only Google's end letter is used

annotation.surface: Someone starting up Google and using the same password again.
annotation.walkthrough: Open sesame is the magic password from Ali Baba; the web-login surface hides that.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the magic words that open the robbers' cave in Ali Baba are the most famous password in fiction.

entries.clue: Occasionally unsteady? That’s not new (4)

indicatorNotes.Occasionally: every other letter, only now and then

annotation.surface: Something wobbly now and then, which is no surprise since it is not new.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' looks like an adverb about wobbling; it picks every other letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: second-hand goods have had an owner before, so are not new.

entries.clue: Antagonism for one appearing in this theatrical production (10)

indicatorNotes.appearing in: an actor appearing in a show is inside the production, so EG goes inside NATIVITY

blocks.note: the nativity play put on by schools at Christmas

annotation.surface: Someone's hostility on show in a stage production.
annotation.walkthrough: A nativity play is the Christmas story staged, usually by schoolchildren.
annotation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a hostile, opposing attitude is antagonism.

entries.clue: Epic march in which one’s gone astray (8,4)

indicatorNotes.in which: the march is something in which the next piece sits, so IS goes inside PARADE

annotation.surface: A long march during which someone wanders off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Epic march' reads as a long trek, but 'Epic' is the definition: Milton's poem.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: Milton's twelve-book poem of the Fall is the great English epic.

entries.clue: Not well kept by vessel with guns (9)

annotation.surface: A sick sailor held aboard a warship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vessel with guns' reads as a warship; the vessel is a blood vessel.
annotation.definitionFit: Collective synonym: large-calibre mounted weapons, taken together, are an army's big guns.

entries.clue: Contender’s sea trawler dismissed as out of order (8)

indicatorNotes.dismissed: sent away, like a player dismissed from the field, so the A's leave the fodder

blocks.note: remove the As, the two letter A's

annotation.surface: A fishing boat owned by a competitor is condemned as broken.
annotation.walkthrough: 'as' reads as a plain conjunction, but here it is A's, the two letter As to drop from SEA TRAWLER.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a grappler in the ring is one kind of contender.

entries.clue: Making sense of some arithmetic (6,2)

blocks.note: said of an explanation that hangs together
totting a column of figures together

annotation.surface: Someone trying to understand a sum.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, understanding maths; it splits into two meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: figuratively a story that hangs together, literally summing numbers.

entries.clue: Ground ready to welcome landlord, finally invited for special occasion (3,6,3)

indicatorNotes.Ground: ground as in ground down, so READY is crushed into new order
indicatorNotes.to welcome: the rearranged letters take LETTER and D inside
indicatorNotes.finally: 'finally' means at the end, so only the end letter of the next word counts

blocks.note: a landlord lets property, so is one who lets

annotation.surface: A prepared field awaits the landlord, the last to be invited to a celebration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a noun, a sports ground, but it is the past participle of grind. The landlord trick is worth learning: one who lets is a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: saints' days were printed in red in church calendars, so a memorable day is marked out as special.

entries.clue: Part of the Bible left wrapped up in thirty seconds? Not by him! (6)

annotation.definitionNote: an extended cross-reference: Milton wrote Paradise Lost (14 across) but not the Bible

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue OT + L read upwards
indicatorNotes.wrapped: MIN wraps round the reversed letters

blocks.note: half a minute is half of MINUTE, MIN

annotation.surface: A pious aside: a bit of scripture is packed in half a minute, and the writer disowns it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thirty seconds' is half of a minute, so half the word MINUTE. The exclamation says Milton wrote a biblical epic but not the Bible.
annotation.definitionFit: John Milton was a poet, famously not the Bible's author though he retold Genesis.

entries.clue: Story of Romeo: literary cliché coming up (6)

indicatorNotes.coming up: in a down clue TROPE reads upwards

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the phonetic alphabet
a trope is a stock literary device

annotation.surface: Romeo's tale is full of worn-out literary devices.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Story of Romeo' makes you think of Shakespeare; 'Story' alone is the definition and Romeo is just R.
annotation.definitionFit: Journalistic synonym: a news item filed by a reporter is a story.

entries.clue: High and mighty people rejected shady character (4)

indicatorNotes.rejected: sent back, so the letters run backwards

annotation.surface: Important people turn away a dodgy type.
annotation.walkthrough: A spiv is British slang for a flashy petty crook, the wartime black-market dealer.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: the flashily dressed wartime black-market dealer is a byword for a shady character.

entries.clue: Putty shaped in its place (10)

indicatorNotes.shaped: the letters are moulded into a new form

annotation.surface: Putty pressed into its proper spot.
annotation.walkthrough: The indicator suits the answer: plasticine is exactly what you shape. Putty is used loosely for any soft modelling paste.
annotation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: the children's modelling clay is soft and pliable like putty.

entries.clue: Kind of bush? That’s about right (5)

blocks.note: the word itself, referred to by 'That'

annotation.surface: Someone asks if a plant is a type of bush and is told that's roughly correct.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That' points back to the word BUSH, which is reused on purpose as fodder; 'about right' sounds like approximate agreement.
annotation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a low woody plant with many stems is what gardeners call a bush.

entries.clue: Male 50 per cent of students (4)

indicatorNotes.50 per cent of: fifty per cent is a half, so only half the word's letters are kept

annotation.surface: A statistic: half of all students are men.
annotation.walkthrough: STUDENTS has eight letters, and the first four make the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A stud is a male animal kept for breeding, or a virile man.

entries.clue: A long way from Blighty earthenware (5-4)

indicatorNotes.from: the letters are taken from the words that follow

annotation.surface: Pottery shipped from home, a long way off.
annotation.walkthrough: Blighty is old British slang for Britain, home to soldiers abroad.
annotation.definitionFit: Unit as distance: the distance light travels in a year, nearly six trillion miles, is a very long way.

entries.clue: Back in a fortnight for the overture (5)

indicatorNotes.in: the letters sit inside the word

annotation.surface: Returning in two weeks' time in order to hear the opening music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back in a fortnight' reads as a promise to return; it hides the answer backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: the clipped form of introduction means the opening piece of music.

entries.clue: Fast kind of music, with nonchalance (7)

blocks.note: idly = in a casual, unconcerned way

annotation.surface: A style of music played quickly but in a laid-back way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast kind of music' reads as one phrase, but 'Fast' stands alone as an adverb.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, both adverbs: to run fast is to run at speed.

entries.clue: A boy, ten playing with weapon (7)

indicatorNotes.playing: the letters play around into a new order

annotation.surface: A ten-year-old boy playing with a weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: The worrying image is the disguise: 'playing' is the instruction to rearrange A BOY TEN.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the blade fixed to a rifle's muzzle is a weapon.
